newsitem.title: USA: Calif. Gov. signs electricity deregulation measure.
newsitem.headline: Calif. Gov. signs electricity deregulation measure.

text.p: California Governor Pete Wilson on Monday signed far-reaching legislation to open the state's massive electricity market to competition and slash consumer rates.
The California state Legislature overwhelmingly approved the deregulation plan in late August. Lawmakers described the measure as "historic" and a "model" for the nation.

The sweeping legislation will restructure the electric industry in California, ending the utility monopoly on generation and opening the market to competition so that retail customers could choose among electric energy suppliers.
"This landmark legislation is a major step in our efforts to guarantee lower rates, provide consumer choice and offer reliable service," Wilson said at the bill signing ceremony.

The bill has the support of the large utilities that would be affected most, Pacific Gas and Electric Co, Enova Corp's San Diego Gas and Electric, and Edison International's Southern California Edison.

Supporters of the legislation said that deregulation would stimulate the state's economy and save California schools over $123 million by the year 2002. Critics contended that the plan was effectively a bailout for powerful utilities.

The legislation lays out a five year transition period during which the state's $21 billion electricity market will be opened to competition. Municipal utilities would not be required to open their markets, but most were expected to comply voluntarily.

To help the investor-owned utilities better compete as the generation market opens, the utilities would be compensated for certain "stranded" costs, such as nuclear power plants, that would not be economical in a competitive market.
They would be compensated through a system-wide competition transition charge.
The legislation authorizes the California Infrastructure Bank to issue up to $10 billion in revenue bonds to help the utilities pay off their stranded costs.
By issuing the bonds through the state bank, the utilities would obtain more favorable interest rates on the debt. State taxpayers would have no obligation or financial exposure.
The bond financings would provide substantial savings to the utilities, and those savings, under the legislation, would be passed on to the customers of utilities in California.

Residential users and small commercial businesses are guaranteed a rate reduction of 10 percent starting January 1, 1998, followed by another 10 percent reduction by 2002, the end of the five year transition period.

"We're doing more than signing a new law, we are shifting the balance of power in California," Wilson said. "We've pulled the plug on another outdated monopoly and replaced it with the promise of a new era of competition."
